These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: MPN: Leveraging Multilingual Patch Neuron for Cross-lingual Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we perform cross-lingual model editing to update knowledge in multilingual models so that edits in one language generalize to other languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple method for cross-lingual model editing by training multilingual patch neurons, which can be easily adapted to existing fine-tuning based editing methods to improve their cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: MPN is an effective method for cross-lingual model editing that enhances cross-lingual generalization while maintaining locality and reliability, requiring minimal changes to existing editing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Existing fine-tuning based editing methods possess a certain degree of cross-lingual editing effect, derived from the inherent cross-lingual transfer ability of the multilingual model.
The proposed MPN method improves cross-lingual editing performance without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology.
MPN achieves an average improvement of about 9% in CLG on the XFEVER dataset and about 12% on the XNLI dataset compared to baselines.
MPN demonstrates strong cross-lingual generalization and good locality, outperforming monolingual editing baselines.
The method is versatile and can be extended to other fine-tuning based editing methods.
papers.limitation:
The cross-lingual editing method is only applied to classification tasks (XFEVER and XNLI) and not to more complex tasks like question-answering.
The XFEVER dataset is created using machine translation without manual verification, which may affect translation quality.
future_direction: Utilize the Bi-zsRE dataset to assess cross-lingual editing performance on question-answering tasks.
Consider using larger models like GPT-4 to potentially improve translation results for dataset creation.
papers.abstract: Large language models are known for encoding a vast amount of factual knowledge, but they often becomes outdated due to the ever-changing nature of external information. A promising solution to this challenge is the utilization of model editing methods to update the knowledge in an efficient manner. However, the majority of existing model editing techniques are limited to monolingual frameworks, thus failing to address the crucial issue of cross-lingual knowledge synchronization for multilingual models. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that trains multilingual patch neuron to store cross-lingual knowledge. It can be easily adapted to existing approaches to enhance their cross-lingual editing capabilities. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments using both the XNLI dataset and a self-constructed XFEVER dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves improved performance in cross-lingual editing tasks without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology, thereby showcasing its user-friendly characteristics. Codes will be released soon.

papers.title: Improving Multilingual Language Models by Aligning Representations through Steering
papers.research_question: How can multilingual alignment in LLMs be achieved efficiently by targeting a single layer through representation steering, and what does this reveal about internal structures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method to enhance multilingual LLMs by steering representations at a single layer, achieving performance competitive with translation systems while requiring fewer resources.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation-level steering is an efficient tool for improving multilingual capabilities, providing insights into internal representations and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer steering significantly improves multilingual performance over baselines like prompt optimization and SFT.
Steering vectors can be shared across structurally similar languages, enabling zero-shot cross-linguistic transfer.
The method approaches the performance of Google Translate, with DPO steering trailing by only 3.08%.
High-resource languages dominate the representation space, and steering helps align low-resource languages.
Steering is most effective in early layers for multilingual models like Aya23, while for models like Llama2, it varies by language resource level.
papers.limitation:
probing by sweeping across all model layers is not scalable for LLMs and is impractical for real-world applications
the learnable steering vector is constrained by its fixed linear direction, limiting its capacity to capture intricate mapping relationships
experiments were focused on single layer and language, lacking multi-objective training
future_direction: Developing context-aware steering mechanisms that adapt dynamically to each prompt
Learning steering vectors by individual tokens rather than fixed vectors
Multi-objective training for simultaneous multi-language and multi-layer steering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent non-English tokens -- a question that remains underexplored despite recent progress. We propose a lightweight intervention method using representation steering, where a learned vector is added to the residual stream at a single model layer to enhance multilingual performance. Through extensive experiments across seven competitive baselines -- including prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in-context learning, cross-lingual transfer, and translation-based methods-we show that our approach consistently outperforms most alternatives. In particular, it achieves performance on par with production-grade translation systems while requiring far fewer resources. We further explore the complementarity between our method and SFT, demonstrating that steering offers a direct, efficient way to realign internal representations. These findings underscore the potential of activation-level interventions as a powerful tool for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Improving In-context Learning of Multilingual Generative Language Models with Cross-lingual Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual in-context learning and mitigate performance bias between languages in multilingual generative models using limited parallel data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a cross-lingual alignment framework (AFP) that uses multilingual contrastive learning and cross-lingual instruction following to improve cross-lingual abilities and reduce performance gaps in multilingual generative models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AFP framework improves cross-lingual capabilities and internal representations of multilingual generative models, reducing performance gaps between languages.
papers.key_findings:
AFP significantly improves cross-lingual in-context learning performance on various tasks with less than 0.1‰ of pre-training tokens.
AFP mitigates the internal representation gap between languages, leading to better-aligned and more uniform multilingual representations.
Cross-lingual instruction following (CIF) is more effective than multilingual instruction tuning (MIT) for cross-lingual ability.
AFP also improves performance on unseen languages for models like Llama that are pre-trained mainly on English.
The framework is effective across different model scales and architectures.
papers.limitation:
Relies on labeled parallel data, which is unavailable for languages without parallel samples.
Limited to models with up to 7.5B parameters due to computational constraints.
Error propagation from the machine translation system used may result in inferior performance.
future_direction: Extend the framework to align different modalities in multi-modal generative models.
Develop unsupervised multilingual alignment methods.
papers.abstract: Multilingual generative models obtain remarkable cross-lingual in-context learning capabilities through pre-training on large-scale corpora. However, they still exhibit a performance bias toward high-resource languages and learn isolated distributions of multilingual sentence representations, which may hinder knowledge transfer across languages. To bridge this gap, we propose a simple yet effective cross-lingual alignment framework exploiting pairs of translation sentences. It aligns the internal sentence representations across different languages via multilingual contrastive learning and aligns outputs by following cross-lingual instructions in the target language. Experimental results show that even with less than 0.1 {\textperthousand} of pre-training tokens, our alignment framework significantly boosts the cross-lingual abilities of generative language models and mitigates the performance gap. Further analyses reveal that it results in a better internal multilingual representation distribution of multilingual models.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: SLAM: Towards Efficient Multilingual Reasoning via Selective Language Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently align multilingual reasoning abilities in large language models while avoiding catastrophic forgetting and reducing computational cost?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SLAM, a method that selectively fine-tunes only the lower-level FFN sub-layers responsible for multilingual comprehension, achieving efficient multilingual reasoning alignment in one stage without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: SLAM efficiently achieves multilingual reasoning alignment by selectively fine-tuning lower-level FFN sub-layers, demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency across multiple tasks and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Lower-level layers are responsible for language-specific representations, while higher-level layers create universal representations.
Selectively fine-tuning FFN sub-layers in the first six layers achieves state-of-the-art multilingual reasoning performance with only 6.5-8% of parameters.
SLAM reduces training time by 4.1-11.9x compared to the two-stage full-parameter tuning method.
SLAM generalizes well to out-of-domain mathematical reasoning and to multilingual common sense reasoning.
Increasing the overlap of activated neurons between non-English and English at lower layers improves multilingual comprehension and reasoning alignment.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are primarily conducted on Llama2 series models, limiting generalizability to other model families.
Imbalanced data among languages in the translation dataset leads to performance trade-offs across languages.
future_direction: Extend experiments to additional series models beyond Llama2.
Conduct in-depth analysis of performance trade-offs across languages due to imbalanced data.
papers.abstract: Despite the significant improvements achieved by large language models (LLMs) in English reasoning tasks, these models continue to struggle with multilingual reasoning. Recent studies leverage a full-parameter and two-stage training paradigm to teach models to first understand non-English questions and then reason. However, this method suffers from both substantial computational resource computing and catastrophic forgetting. The fundamental cause is that, with the primary goal of enhancing multilingual comprehension, an excessive number of irrelevant layers and parameters are tuned during the first stage. Given our findings that the representation learning of languages is merely conducted in lower-level layers, we propose an efficient multilingual reasoning alignment approach that precisely identifies and fine-tunes the layers responsible for handling multilingualism. Experimental results show that our method, SLAM, only tunes 6 layers' feed-forward sub-layers including 6.5-8% of all parameters within 7B and 13B LLMs, achieving superior average performance than all strong baselines across 10 languages. Meanwhile, SLAM only involves one training stage, reducing training time by 4.1-11.9 compared to the two-stage method.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Not All Neural Embeddings are Born Equal
papers.research_question: How does the architecture/objective function of neural models affect the information encoded in their word embeddings, specifically comparing translation-based and monolingual embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Translation-based word embeddings outperform monolingual embeddings on tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and syntactic role, suggesting the translation objective better captures the ontological status of concepts.
papers.conclusion: Neural machine translation models learn word embeddings that more effectively encode conceptual similarity and syntactic role information compared to monolingual models, likely due to the cross-lingual alignment pressure of the translation objective.
papers.key_findings:
Translation-based embeddings achieve higher correlation on SimLex-999 (similarity) and higher accuracy on the TOEFL synonym test and synonym/antonym classification compared to monolingual embeddings.
Monolingual embeddings perform better on relatedness tasks (WordSim-353, MEN).
Translation-based embeddings excel at syntactic analogies, while monolingual embeddings are better at semantic analogies.
The performance advantage of translation-based embeddings on similarity tasks is not due to training data quantity, as monolingual models trained on larger corpora do not match their performance.
The translation objective may induce embeddings that better approximate ontological similarity by aligning words across languages, even when their co-occurrence patterns differ.
papers.abstract: Neural language models learn word representations that capture rich linguistic and conceptual information. Here we investigate the embeddings learned by neural machine translation models. We show that translation-based embeddings outperform those learned by cutting-edge monolingual models at single-language tasks requiring knowledge of conceptual similarity and/or syntactic role. The findings suggest that, while monolingual models learn information about how concepts are related, neural-translation models better capture their true ontological status.

papers.title: Isolating Culture Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we localize a set of neurons that drives cultural propensities in multilingual LLMs, separate them from language-specific neurons, and modulate them through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that culture-specific neurons can be identified in multilingual LLMs, are largely separable from language-specific neurons, and can be selectively modulated through interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cultural knowledge concentrates in specialized neuron populations predominantly localized in upper layers of multilingual language models and that pure culture neurons play a substantial functional role.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-specific neurons are largely separable from language-specific neurons.
Cultural representations are localized in upper layers of the model.
Different cultures are encoded in distinct neural populations with minimal cross-cultural interference.
Pure culture-specific neurons (not overlapping with language) constitute about 56.7% of culture-related neurons and are functionally important.
Ablation of culture-specific neurons increases perplexity on culturally relevant data, confirming their critical role.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to a small set of open-source models.
Methodology relies on entropy-based metrics and dataset sampling choices.
MUREL covers only six cultures, potentially omitting important cultural phenomena.
Evaluation focuses on neuron ablation and perplexity; future work should include more comprehensive behavioral and downstream assessments.
future_direction: Broadening coverage to additional cultures, languages, and models.
Extending localization to attention heads.
Testing sufficiency via activation scaling and steering, and evaluating intervention effects on downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Language and culture are deeply intertwined, yet it has been unclear how and where multilingual large language models encode culture. Here, we build on an established methodology for identifying language-specific neurons to localize and isolate culture-specific neurons, carefully disentangling their overlap and interaction with language-specific neurons. To facilitate our experiments, we introduce MUREL, a curated dataset of 85.2 million tokens spanning six different cultures. Our localization and intervention experiments show that LLMs encode different cultures in distinct neuron populations, predominantly in upper layers, and that these culture neurons can be modulated largely independently of language-specific neurons or those specific to other cultures. These findings suggest that cultural knowledge and propensities in multilingual language models can be selectively isolated and edited, with implications for fairness, inclusivity, and alignment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/namazifard/Culture_Neurons.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models? Is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representation in multilingual models consists of both shared and language-specific components. The most dominant gender directions are shared across languages, enabling good cross-lingual gender classification, but language-specific directions prevent effective cross-lingual gender removal.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared and less salient ones being language-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification using linear probes transfers well across languages (English, French, Spanish).
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared gender directions are the most dominant ones (highest predictive power).
The partial sharing explains the discrepancy between transferable classification and non-transferable removal.
papers.limitation:
The study relies on a narrow, binary notion of gender, which does not reflect the full complexity of gender bias.
The analysis is limited to three languages (English, French, Spanish) due to dataset availability.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.research_question: Can explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages enhance cross-lingual generalization in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) are implicitly alignable across languages in transformer LMs, and proposes a meta-learning method to explicitly align these concepts, improving zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual generalization without updating the LM parameters.
papers.conclusion: Explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages via meta-learning improves cross-lingual generalization, achieving competitive performance and narrowing the gap between languages, particularly for low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
Structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) can be identified based on prototypes in a relatively low-dimensional space of LM representations.
These structural concepts are highly alignable across languages in both encoder-only (mBERT) and decoder-only (LLaMA) models, as measured by RSA and Procrustes analysis.
A meta-learning-based method to align conceptual spaces achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on syntactic analysis tasks, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
The method reduces the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages.
The approach provides insights into cross-lingual in-context learning and can be integrated with prompting to improve generalization.
papers.limitation: Variations in alignability between language pairs may stem from insufficient UD treebank data for approximating prototypes and degenerate representation spaces for certain languages due to inadequate pretraining data or tokenization deficiencies.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to other aspects of language to better accommodate linguistic diversity using self-supervised knowledge.
Exploring more expressive probing models to extract structural concepts, especially grammatical relations, from models like LLaMA.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.

papers.title: Viewing Knowledge Transfer in Multilingual Machine Translation Through a Representational Lens
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual knowledge transfer and representational similarities in multilingual neural machine translation, and can we develop a better measure for transfer than translation quality alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), a measure of knowledge transfer based on representational similarities between languages in multilingual machine translation, and proposes a novel training scheme with an auxiliary similarity loss that improves translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) is a better measure of knowledge transfer than translation quality alone, and that explicitly optimizing for language invariance using multi-parallel data improves translation for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) can measure both positive and negative transfer and is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality (BLEU), indicating that improvements are due to knowledge transfer and not just increased target data.
Multi-parallel overlap between languages is a highly predictive yet under-explored feature for transfer.
A training method that uses an auxiliary similarity loss to encourage language-invariant representations yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.
RTP can be used to identify suitable auxiliary transfer languages, with training on top RTP contributors leading to substantially better results than training on bottom contributors.
Dataset features (multi-parallel overlap, source subword overlap, vocabulary occupancy) are more predictive of representational similarity than linguistic features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English-centric many-to-many and many-to-English models, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other multilingual settings.
The training data size (TED corpus) is relatively small compared to other datasets like OPUS-100, which may affect model performance.
papers.abstract: We argue that translation quality alone is not a sufficient metric for measuring knowledge transfer in multilingual neural machine translation. To support this claim, we introduce Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), which measures representational similarities between languages. We show that RTP can measure both positive and negative transfer (interference), and find that RTP is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality, indicating that transfer does occur. Furthermore, we investigate data and language characteristics that are relevant for transfer, and find that multi-parallel overlap is an important yet under-explored feature. Based on this, we develop a novel training scheme, which uses an auxiliary similarity loss that encourages representations to be more invariant across languages by taking advantage of multi-parallel data. We show that our method yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.

papers.title: Exploring Representational Disparities Between Multilingual and Bilingual Translation Models
papers.research_question: How does the ambient space utilization of model representations differ between bilingual models and one-to-many models? If space utilization differs, what might be driving these differences?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than bilingual decoder representations, largely due to language-specific information occupying representational capacity.
papers.conclusion: There is a consistent reduction in representational capacity in multilingual decoders versus bilingual decoders, attributed to language information occupying a significant portion of the representation space.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual decoder representations are less isotropic than bilingual decoder representations across different data resource levels and language pairs.
Multilingual encoder representations are slightly more isotropic than bilingual encoder representations, but the improvement is smaller than the decoder reduction.
The reduction in multilingual decoder isotropy is driven by language-specific information occupying much of the available representation space.
Isotropy decreases with larger training scale, related to the representation degeneration problem.
In multiparallel data, the decoder isotropy reduction is less pronounced for related languages (e.g., Russian and Ukrainian).
papers.limitation:
Models cover at most 3 language families, while modern multilingual translation models cover many more.
Focus on one-to-many models, but many-to-many models may have different behavior.
Focus on encoder-decoder models, but decoder-only translation models may differ.
Work focuses on characterization, not on improving representational capacity.
future_direction: Analyze models with larger language coverage.
Investigate many-to-many multilingual models.
Study decoder-only translation models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual machine translation has proven immensely useful for both parameter efficiency and overall performance across many language pairs via complete multilingual parameter sharing. However, some language pairs in multilingual models can see worse performance than in bilingual models, especially in the one-to-many translation setting. Motivated by their empirical differences, we examine the geometric differences in representations from bilingual models versus those from one-to-many multilingual models. Specifically, we compute the isotropy of these representations using intrinsic dimensionality and IsoScore, in order to measure how the representations utilize the dimensions in their underlying vector space. Using the same evaluation data in both models, we find that for a given language pair, its multilingual model decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than comparable bilingual model decoder representations. Additionally, we show that much of the anisotropy in multilingual decoder representations can be attributed to modeling language-specific information, therefore limiting remaining representational capacity.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: The Emergence of Abstract Thought in Large Language Models Beyond Any Language
papers.research_question: Do LLMs think in the distinct space of each language, or do they operate in a higher-level language-agnostic space beyond any specific language? Does the trend of non-English performance compared to English indicate the emergence of abstract thought within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space (shared neurons) that underlies generalization across languages and supports abstract thought. Based on this, neuron-specific training strategies are proposed to enhance multilingual capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Shared neurons form a compact, language-agnostic set that supports abstract reasoning across languages, and neuron-specific training strategies can enhance multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proportion of language-shared neurons increases with model evolution and correlates with multilingual ability.
Language-shared neurons become more functionally important than language-exclusive neurons, evolving into language-agnostic neurons that support abstract thought.
Neuron-targeted training based on the language-agnostic score effectively improves multilingual performance, with different strategies for models at different developmental stages.
papers.limitation: Limited by computational resources, restricting evaluation on larger LLMs and full exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
future_direction: Evaluation on larger LLMs and exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance, their capacity to function effectively across a diverse range of languages has shown marked improvement. Preliminary studies observe that the hidden activations of LLMs often resemble English, even when responding to non-English prompts. This has led to the widespread assumption that LLMs may "think" in English. However, more recent results showing strong multilingual performance, even surpassing English performance on specific tasks in other languages, challenge this view. In this work, we find that LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space-a remarkably small subset of parameters whose deactivation results in significant performance degradation across all languages. This compact yet critical set of parameters underlies the model's ability to generalize beyond individual languages, supporting the emergence of abstract thought that is not tied to any specific linguistic system. Specifically, we identify language-related neurons-those are consistently activated during the processing of particular languages, and categorize them as either shared (active across multiple languages) or exclusive (specific to one). As LLMs undergo continued development over time, we observe a marked increase in both the proportion and functional importance of shared neurons, while exclusive neurons progressively diminish in influence. These shared neurons constitute the backbone of the core language-agnostic parameter space, supporting the emergence of abstract thought. Motivated by these insights, we propose neuron-specific training strategies tailored to LLMs' language-agnostic levels at different development stages. Experiments across diverse LLM families support our approach.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
