papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: A Closer Look at Transformer Attention for Multilingual Translation
papers.research_question: How do multilingual Transformer models pay attention when translating different language pairs? We analyze the functions and behaviors of attention heads in self-attention and cross-attention.
papers.core_contribution: Different language pairs tend to share the same attention heads for functions like syntax and reordering, but language interference reduces head accuracies. Additionally, deep-layer cross-attention heads cooperate to learn multiple reordering options due to multiple valid translations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual Transformer models share attention heads for similar functions across languages, but language interference reduces head accuracies. Deep-layer cross-attention heads cooperate to handle multiple valid reorderings in translation.
papers.key_findings:
Different language pairs share the same attention heads for functions such as syntax and reordering.
Language interference in multilingual models reduces the accuracy of function heads compared to bilingual models.
Deep-layer cross-attention heads work cooperatively to learn different options for word reordering, likely because there are multiple valid translations for a source sentence.
The Transformer decoder uses shallow-layer cross-attention heads for current word alignment and deep-layer heads for next word alignment.
Automatic pruning can remove a large fraction of attention heads without significant loss in translation quality.
papers.limitation: The study covers only six translation directions with limited typological diversity, due to the need for ground truth word alignments.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual models covering many more languages with more linguistic diversity following the same methodology.
papers.abstract: Transformers are the predominant model for machine translation. Recent works also showed that a single Transformer model can be trained to learn translation for multiple different language pairs, achieving promising results. In this work, we investigate how the multilingual Transformer model pays attention for translating different language pairs. We first performed automatic pruning to eliminate a large number of noisy heads and then analyzed the functions and behaviors of the remaining heads in both self-attention and cross-attention. We find that different language pairs, in spite of having different syntax and word orders, tended to share the same heads for the same functions, such as syntax heads and reordering heads. However, the different characteristics of different language pairs clearly caused interference in function heads and affected head accuracies. Additionally, we reveal an interesting behavior of the Transformer cross-attention: the deep-layer cross-attention heads work in a clear cooperative way to learn different options for word reordering, which can be caused by the nature of translation tasks having multiple different gold translations in the target language for the same source sentence.

papers.title: Getting More from Less: Large Language Models are Good Spontaneous Multilingual Learners
papers.research_question: Can LLMs achieve better multilingual alignment across different languages efficiently through instruction-tuning on question translation data without annotated answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs instruction-tuned on question translation data without annotated answers show significant multilingual alignment improvement across a wide range of languages, including unseen languages, demonstrating efficient multilingual capability improvement with great language and task generalization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs trained on question translation data without answers achieve significant multilingual alignment improvement across many languages, including unseen ones, showing great potential for efficient multilingual capability improvement.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models can learn to handle multilingualism better spontaneously through question alignment.
High-resource languages are not only good learners but also good leaders for alignment.
A few languages can lead to spontaneous multilingual learning with great language generalization.
Findings remain consistent across models of different parameter sizes.
English is not necessary as the target language in the training data; Chinese also works.
papers.limitation:
Using few-shot learning; analyzing in a zero-shot setting would strengthen conclusions.
Experiments limited to models up to 14B parameters; verification on larger models (70B+) is needed.
Use of automatic translation engine; data annotated by native speakers would be more accurate.
future_direction: Analyzing multilingual alignment in a zero-shot setting.
Verifying conclusions on larger LLMs (70B or larger).
Using data annotated by native speakers for better accuracy.
papers.abstract: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive language capabilities. While most of the existing LLMs have very unbalanced performance across different languages, multilingual alignment based on translation parallel data is an effective method to enhance the LLMs' multilingual capabilities. In this work, we discover and comprehensively investigate the spontaneous multilingual alignment improvement of LLMs. We find that LLMs instruction-tuned on the question translation data (i.e. without annotated answers) are able to encourage the alignment between English and a wide range of languages, even including those unseen during instruction-tuning. Additionally, we utilize different settings and mechanistic interpretability methods to analyze the LLM's performance in the multilingual scenario comprehensively. Our work suggests that LLMs have enormous potential for improving multilingual alignment efficiently with great language and task generalization.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Soteria: Language-Specific Functional Parameter Steering for Multilingual Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we ensure consistent safety across multiple languages in large language models by locating and minimally adjusting language-specific functional parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Soteria, a lightweight method that identifies and adjusts language-specific functional attention heads to improve multilingual safety alignment by modifying only ~3% of parameters, reducing harmful outputs without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: Soteria provides an effective, parameter-efficient path to scalable multilingual safety alignment, enhancing model safety across diverse languages without compromising utility.
papers.key_findings:
Soteria significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages on safety benchmarks like MultiJail and XThreatBench.
The method outperforms baseline safety alignment techniques such as Safety Arithmetic, Resta, and TIES.
Modifying only the O-projection weights of identified functional heads preserves general model capabilities, as shown by stable MMLU scores.
Attention head analysis reveals that high- and mid-resource languages share functional heads in mid-layers, while low-resource languages utilize heads in later layers.
The approach is robust against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks like POATE and RDR.
papers.limitation:
Relies on per-language functional neuron identification, which requires accurate language segmentation and task-based data in each target language; resource constraints and data limitations can reduce selection precision.
Does not guarantee comprehensive coverage of every cultural nuance or emergent harmful behavior.
future_direction: Investigating attention-head analysis to tackle task-specific heads, misalignment, and hallucination issues.
Enhancing universal attention heads to improve cross-lingual understanding and zero-shot performance for underrepresented languages.
Refining or shifting the latent space of problematic heads to improve overall alignment and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Ensuring consistent safety across multiple languages remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs). We introduce Soteria, a lightweight yet powerful strategy that locates and minimally adjusts the "functional heads" most responsible for harmful content generation in each language. By altering only a fraction of parameters, Soteria drastically reduces policy violations without sacrificing overall model performance, even in low-resource settings. To rigorously evaluate our approach, we also present XThreatBench, a specialized multilingual dataset capturing fine-grained harmful behaviors drawn from real policy guidelines. Experiments with leading open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral) show that Soteria consistently improves safety metrics across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. These findings highlight a promising path toward scalable, linguistically attuned, and ethically aligned LLMs worldwide.

papers.title: Similarity of Sentence Representations in Multilingual LMs: Resolving Conflicting Literature and a Case Study of Baltic Languages
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models internally represent different languages, and do they converge to a shared cross-lingual space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper resolves conflicting literature by showing that multilingual LMs project languages into a shared cross-lingual space when using mean-pooling and CKA/SVCCA, and finds that Baltic languages are part of this space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mean-pooling with SVCCA/CKA is optimal for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis, and while most languages share a cross-lingual space, Baltic languages are part of it.
papers.key_findings:
CLS-pooling with PWCCA gives divergent patterns, while mean-pooling with CKA/SVCCA shows convergence in cross-lingual similarity.
Mean-pooling is more effective than CLS-pooling for cross-lingual representational analysis, as shown by probing tasks.
Not all languages share the cross-lingual space equally; some like Urdu and Hindi are outliers.
Baltic languages (Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian) are grouped and belong to the shared cross-lingual space.
The most cross-lingual layer for XLM-R is the 7th layer.
future_direction: Finding the exact criteria for exclusion of languages from the shared cross-lingual space.
papers.abstract: Low-resource languages, such as Baltic languages, benefit from Large Multilingual Models (LMs) that possess remarkable cross-lingual transfer performance capabilities. This work is an interpretation and analysis study into cross-lingual representations of Multilingual LMs. Previous works hypothesized that these LMs internally project representations of different languages into a shared cross-lingual space. However, the literature produced contradictory results. In this paper, we revisit the prior work claiming that "BERT is not an Interlingua" and show that different languages do converge to a shared space in such language models with another choice of pooling strategy or similarity index. Then, we perform cross-lingual representational analysis for the two most popular multilingual LMs employing 378 pairwise language comparisons. We discover that while most languages share joint cross-lingual space, some do not. However, we observe that Baltic languages do belong to that shared space.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Language-Specific Layer Matters: Efficient Multilingual Enhancement for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently enhance the multilingual capabilities of large vision-language models by identifying and fine-tuning language-specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PLAST, a method to efficiently enhance multilingual capabilities of LVLMs by identifying language-specific layers and fine-tuning them with translation pairs.
papers.conclusion: PLAST effectively enhances multilingual performance of LVLMs and achieves superior efficiency compared to full-parameter tuning methods by fine-tuning only language-specific layers.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons in shallow layers are crucial for multilingual understanding in LVLMs.
PLAST improves multilingual performance with only 14% of parameters tuned, achieving significant efficiency gains.
PLAST generalizes to low-resource languages and complex visual reasoning tasks.
Fine-tuning both FFN and attention sub-layers within selected layers yields better performance than tuning only one.
PLAST outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient methods like LoRA in both performance and efficiency.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 13B parameters due to computing resources.
Performance trade-offs exist across different languages, potentially due to imbalances in multilingual training data.
future_direction: Explore PLAST on larger-scale models (larger than 13B).
Investigate data-centric strategies such as data selection and augmentation to further improve multilingual capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in understanding visual information with human languages but also exhibit an imbalance in multilingual capabilities. In this work, we delve into the multilingual working pattern of LVLMs and identify a salient correlation between the multilingual understanding ability of LVLMs and language-specific neuron activations in shallow layers. Building on this insight, we introduce PLAST, a training recipe that achieves efficient multilingual enhancement for LVLMs by Precise LAnguage-Specific layers fine-Tuning. PLAST first identifies layers involved in multilingual understanding by monitoring language-specific neuron activations. These layers are then precisely fine-tuned with question-translation pairs to achieve multilingual alignment. Our empirical results on MM-Bench and MMMB demonstrate that PLAST effectively improves the multilingual capabilities of LVLMs and achieves significant efficiency with only 14% of the parameters tuned. Further analysis reveals that PLAST can be generalized to low-resource and complex visual reasoning tasks, facilitating the language-specific visual information engagement in shallow layers.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: CRANE: Causal Relevance Analysis of Language-Specific Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are language capabilities organized at the neuron level in multilingual LLMs? The paper redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity and proposes a method to identify language-specific neurons.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRANE, a relevance-based framework for identifying language-specific neurons by functional necessity, and finds asymmetric, language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations in multilingual LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CRANE provides a framework for studying language-specific neurons based on functional necessity, revealing that language-specific neurons are language-selective but non-exclusive, and highlighting the importance of distinguishing statistical correlation from functional contribution.
papers.key_findings:
CRANE induces targeted functional degradation on the intended language while preserving performance on non-target languages, outperforming activation-based methods like LAPE.
Neuron-level interventions reveal an asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations.
Normalized kurtosis of relevance distributions reveals language-related structure in neuron contributions.
Neuron sets identified on the Base model retain functional influence when transferred to the Chat model, indicating partial preservation of language-specific neurons after instruction tuning.
The proposed LangSpec-F1 metric quantifies language-selective functional effects under neuron intervention.
papers.limitation:
CRANE currently relies on normalized kurtosis to characterize concentration patterns in language-conditioned relevance distributions, which is only one possible statistic.
Functional validation is performed via neuron masking, a relatively coarse intervention; more fine-grained causal techniques may provide deeper insight.
Experiments focus on three languages and a single model family, and open-ended generation evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol which may introduce variance.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to broader language coverage, additional architectures, and alternative evaluation paradigms.
Using more fine-grained causal techniques, such as neuron re-weighting or path-specific analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across languages, yet how language capabilities are organized at the neuron level remains poorly understood. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. We propose CRANE, a relevance-based analysis framework that redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity, identifying language-specific neurons through targeted neuron-level interventions. CRANE characterizes neuron specialization by their contribution to language-conditioned predictions rather than activation magnitude. Our implementation will be made publicly available. Neuron-level interventions reveal a consistent asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages to a substantial extent, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations. Experiments on English, Chinese, and Vietnamese across multiple benchmarks, together with a dedicated relevance-based metric and base-to-chat model transfer analysis, show that CRANE isolates language-specific components more precisely than activation-based methods.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: How Language Directions Align with Token Geometry in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Where and how is language information encoded within transformer layers? Does the pretraining language distribution structurally reshape the geometry of multilingual representations?
papers.core_contribution: Language information in multilingual LLMs is linearly separable from the first transformer block and remains stable across layers, and the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is shaped by pretraining data composition, indicating structural imprinting.
papers.conclusion: Language representation in LLMs is distinguished by latent representational structures formed during pretraining, established early and preserved across layers, highlighting the importance of balanced language composition for fairness and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4±8.2%p from Layer 0→1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth.
The alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data, with Chinese-inclusive models showing 4.21× higher alignment for Chinese compared to English-centric models.
Chinese reaches maximal separability in deeper layers, whereas Spanish and German converge earlier, showing typological effects.
Linear probes achieve 99.8±0.1% accuracy on average, with only a 0.58±0.12%p gap relative to MLP probes, indicating linear separability.
Match@Peak remains low for Latin-script languages, suggesting language directions capture abstract features beyond token identity.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five languages and may not generalize to all languages or scripts.
future_direction: expanding the analysis to additional languages and scripts
evaluating the influence of tokenizer design
conducting interventional studies
papers.abstract: Multilingual LLMs demonstrate strong performance across diverse languages, yet there has been limited systematic analysis of how language information is structured within their internal representation space and how it emerges across layers. We conduct a comprehensive probing study on six multilingual LLMs, covering all 268 transformer layers, using linear and nonlinear probes together with a new Token--Language Alignment analysis to quantify the layer-wise dynamics and geometric structure of language encoding. Our results show that language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4$\pm$8.2 percentage points from Layer 0 to 1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth. We further find that the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data. Notably, Chinese-inclusive models achieve a ZH Match@Peak of 16.43\%, whereas English-centric models achieve only 3.90\%, revealing a 4.21$\times$ structural imprinting effect. These findings indicate that multilingual LLMs distinguish languages not by surface script features but by latent representational structures shaped by the training corpus. Our analysis provides practical insights for data composition strategies and fairness in multilingual representation learning. All code and analysis scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/thisiskorea/How-Language-Directions-Align-with-Token-Geometry-in-Multilingual-LLMs.

papers.title: Enhancing Multilingual Text Understanding viaTransformer-Based Meta-Learning
papers.research_question: How can multilingual text understanding be enhanced by integrating structured linguistic knowledge (syntactic and semantic) into transformer-based models via meta-learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning via a Grammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, enhancing multilingual text understanding by aligning neural attention mechanisms with syntactic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA into a transformer-based meta-learning framework significantly improves multilingual text understanding, though limitations exist in handling noisy language and reliance on syntactic annotations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model (LexiStruct with GIRA) outperforms baseline methods on multiple multilingual benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, TyDiQAt, WikiAnn) across metrics like NDCG, Recall, MRR, and Hit Rate.
Ablation studies show that key components (Syntactic Structure Injection, Syntax-Semantics Alignment, Grammar-Semantics Alignment) are essential for the model's performance, with removal of any leading to significant drops in metrics.
The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA improves the model's robustness and interpretability in multilingual understanding tasks.
papers.limitation:
The integration of grammatical constraints may reduce the model's flexibility in handling less-structured or noisy language inputs, such as colloquialisms or code-switching phenomena.
The current implementation assumes access to high-quality syntactic annotations, which may not be available for all languages, especially low-resource ones.
future_direction: Explore strategies for relaxing the assumption of high-quality syntactic annotations, possibly through unsupervised or semi-supervised learning of syntactic structures.
Extend the model's adaptability to more diverse and informal language domains to improve broader applicability in real-world multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the evolving landscape of computational sciences, the integration of structured linguistic knowledge into deep learningmodels has become increasingly vital for advancing multilingual text understanding. Traditional transformer-based architectures,while powerful, often lack the capacity to inherently capture the syntactic and semantic nuances present across diverselanguages, leading to limitations in generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novelframework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning. Our approach employsa structure-aware neural language model that incorporates grammatical constraints directly into the learning process,enhancing the model’s ability to comprehend and process multilingual data effectively. Central to our methodology is theGrammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, which aligns neural attention mechanisms with syntacticdependencies, ensuring that the model’s internal representations adhere to linguistic structures. Experimental evaluationsdemonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in multilingual understanding tasks, exhibiting enhanced robustnessinterpretability. This work contributes to the field by offering a principled method that bridges the gap between statistical learningand linguistic theory, aligning with the journal’s commitment to advancing both fundamental and applied computational sciences.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance
papers.research_question: How do language models generalize knowledge to multiple languages, and why do they produce inconsistent outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs tend to reason in language-specific subspaces, hindering cross-lingual consistency and transfer, while smaller models rely on a shared English-aligned semantic space; steering smaller models towards this shared space improves their multilingual performance.
papers.conclusion: The use of shared semantic space facilitates cross-lingual transfer, and inducing processing in this space can improve multilingual reasoning in smaller models.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models are more accurate but less consistent across languages.
Cross-lingual representation similarity predicts knowledge transfer and consistency.
Larger models operate more in language-specific subspaces, while smaller models use a shared English-aligned space.
Cross-lingual activation steering towards English improves performance and consistency in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
The steering method is only tested on multi-choice questions and requires extraction of language-specific activation vectors, which may not generalize to other use cases.
The method may reinforce cultural and linguistic biases towards English.
future_direction: Develop more comprehensive methods to encode knowledge of different languages in the shared semantic space.
Address the limitation of reinforcing English bias in multilingual models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are demonstrably capable of cross-lingual transfer, but can produce inconsistent output when prompted with the same queries written in different languages. To understand how language models are able to generalize knowledge from one language to the others, we measure representation similarity between languages, and apply the logit lens to interpret the implicit steps taken by LLMs to solve multilingual multi-choice reasoning questions. Our analyses reveal LLMs predict inconsistently and are less accurate because they rely on representations that are dissimilar across languages, rather than working in a shared semantic space. While larger models are more multilingual, we show their hidden states are more likely to dissociate from the shared representation compared to smaller models, but are nevertheless more capable of retrieving knowledge embedded across different languages. Finally, we demonstrate that knowledge sharing in small models can be facilitated by steering their latent processing towards the shared semantic space. This improves the models' multilingual reasoning performance, as a result of more knowledge transfer from, and better output consistency with English.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: It’s not Greek to mBERT: Inducing Word-Level Translations from Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How much word-level translation information is recoverable by multilingual BERT (mBERT) and how is this information stored?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual BERT encodes word-level translation information that can be extracted via simple template-based and analogies-based methods without fine-tuning, and identifies a language-identity subspace in its representations.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge needed for word-level translation is implicitly encoded in mBERT and is easy to extract with simple methods without fine-tuning; this information is likely stored non-linearly, though some parts can be recovered linearly via a language-identity subspace.
papers.key_findings:
The template-based method achieves high accuracy in word-level translation without any fine-tuning.
The analogies-based method, which manipulates language-encoding components via vector arithmetic, also performs well, indicating some translation information is linearly recoverable.
mBERT representations can be decomposed into language-encoding and language-neutral components using INLP.
An empirical language-identity subspace can be identified within mBERT representations, where representations are well-separated by language.
Most translation information in mBERT is stored non-linearly, but a portion is linearly accessible.
future_direction: Further investigation of the sources of the template-based method's success.
papers.abstract: Recent works have demonstrated that multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns rich cross-lingual representations, that allow for transfer across languages. We study the word-level translation information embedded in mBERT and present two simple methods that expose remarkable translation capabilities with no finetuning. The results suggest that most of this information is encoded in a non-linear way, while some of it can also be recovered with purely linear tools. As part of our analysis, we test the hypothesis that mBERT learns representations which contain both a languageencoding component and an abstract, crosslingual component, and explicitly identify an empirical language-identity subspace within mBERT representations.

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: On the Entity-Level Alignment in Crosslingual Consistency
papers.research_question: What factors give rise to crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and do failures in entity alignment cause inconsistencies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis linking crosslingual consistency to entity-level alignment, introduces two prompting methods (SUBSUB and SUBINJ) that improve factual recall and consistency, and uses mechanistic interpretability to show these methods enhance entity representation alignment through pivot-language processing.
papers.conclusion: Entity alignment is a key factor underlying crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and the proposed prompting methods offer effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction by enhancing this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Crosslingual consistency is strongly correlated with entity alignment across all studied models.
Consistent factual recall rarely occurs without correctly aligning either the subject or object entities between two languages.
The proposed prompting methods SUBSUB and SUBINJ, which incorporate English translations of subjects, substantially improve factual recall accuracy and consistency, especially in English-centric models.
Mechanistic analysis using Logit Lens shows that SUBSUB and SUBINJ interventions reinforce entity representation alignment in the model's internal conceptual space.
The model's conceptual space is biased towards high-resource languages like English, explaining why using English subject translations is more effective than using other languages.
papers.limitation: Inconsistency can also stem from failure in the processing stage – i.e., the model lacks the factual knowledge so it cannot retrieve the correct object in the conceptual space, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are expected to recall factual knowledge consistently across languages. However, the factors that give rise to such crosslingual consistency -- and its frequent failure -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we hypothesize that these inconsistencies may arise from failures in entity alignment, the process of mapping subject and object entities into a shared conceptual space across languages. To test this, we assess alignment through entity-level (subject and object) translation tasks, and find that consistency is strongly correlated with alignment across all studied models, with misalignment of subjects or objects frequently resulting in inconsistencies. Building on this insight, we propose SubSub and SubInj, two effective methods that integrate English translations of subjects into prompts across languages, leading to substantial gains in both factual recall accuracy and consistency. Finally, our mechanistic analysis reveals that these interventions reinforce the entity representation alignment in the conceptual space through model's internal pivot-language processing, offering effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction.

papers.title: Probing Cross-Lingual Lexical Knowledge from Multilingual Sentence Encoders
papers.research_question: How to best leverage multilingual sentence encoders to represent sub-sentence lexical items (words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks, and how much cross-lingual lexical knowledge is stored in their parameters.
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via an inexpensive contrastive learning procedure requiring only a small dictionary, exposing more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than is available when using them off-the-shelf.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that multilingual sentence encoders can be effectively transformed into cross-lingual lexical encoders via contrastive fine-tuning, exposing rich lexical knowledge that is particularly beneficial for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual sentence encoders (LaBSE, XMPNET) store more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than vanilla multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).
Contrastive cross-lingual lexical fine-tuning with a small dictionary (1k-5k pairs) substantially improves performance on lexical tasks like BLI, XLSIM, and XEL.
Interpolating the fine-tuned encoder representations with static cross-lingual word embeddings (CLWEs) yields further performance gains, especially for low-resource language pairs.
The gains from contrastive fine-tuning are particularly large for low-resource language pairs, indicating the stored lexical knowledge is crucial in data-scarce scenarios.
Multilingual sentence encoders are more resilient to training data scarcity than static CLWE methods like VECMAP.
papers.abstract: Pretrained multilingual language models (LMs) can be successfully transformed into multilingual sentence encoders (SEs; e.g., LaBSE, xMPNet) via additional fine-tuning or model distillation with parallel data. However, it remains unclear how to best leverage them to represent sub-sentence lexical items (i.e., words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks. In this work, we probe SEs for the amount of cross-lingual lexical knowledge stored in their parameters, and compare them against the original multilingual LMs. We also devise a simple yet efficient method for exposing the cross-lingual lexical knowledge by means of additional fine-tuning through inexpensive contrastive learning that requires only a small amount of word translation pairs. Using bilingual lexical induction (BLI), cross-lingual lexical semantic similarity, and cross-lingual entity linking as lexical probing tasks, we report substantial gains on standard benchmarks (e.g., +10 Precision@1 points in BLI). The results indicate that the SEs such as LaBSE can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via the contrastive learning procedure, and that they contain more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than what 'meets the eye' when they are used as off-the-shelf SEs. This way, we also provide an effective tool for harnessing 'covert' multilingual lexical knowledge hidden in multilingual sentence encoders.

papers.title: The Case for Translation-Invariant Self-Attention in Transformer-Based\n Language Models
papers.research_question: How are positional information encoded in transformer-based language models, and can translation-invariant self-attention be an effective alternative to conventional position embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), a new positional encoding method that satisfies six design criteria and improves performance on GLUE tasks with very few added parameters.
papers.conclusion: Translation invariance emerges in state-of-the-art language models, and TISA is a positional encoding method that satisfies all six design criteria and improves downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Position embeddings in transformer-based language models become increasingly translation-invariant during training, and this invariance correlates with model performance.
Adding TISA to ALBERT improves performance on GLUE tasks with minimal parameter increase.
TISA can be used with or without conventional position embeddings, though performance is better when combined.
papers.limitation:
Lack of computational resources to pretrain TISA-only models from scratch
TISA alone (without position embeddings) does not perform as well as when combined with position embeddings
future_direction: Applying TISA to transformer models in other domains like speech, motion synthesis, and computer vision
Exploring two-stage training with TISA, pre-training on short sequences and then scaling to longer ones
papers.abstract:
Mechanisms for encoding positional information are central for
transformer-based language models. In this paper, we analyze the position
embeddings of existing language models, finding strong evidence of translation
invariance, both for the embeddings themselves and for their effect on
self-attention. The degree of translation invariance increases during training
and correlates positively with model performance. Our findings lead us to
propose translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), which accounts for the
relative position between tokens in an interpretable fashion without needing
conventional position embeddings. Our proposal has several theoretical
advantages over existing position-representation approaches. Experiments show
that it improves on regular ALBERT on GLUE tasks, while only adding orders of
magnitude less positional parameters.

papers.title: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts across modalities
papers.research_question: Do language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across different input modalities (text and images)?
papers.core_contribution: Language models predict brain activity better in regions with high semantic consistency across modalities, even when those regions are not language-selective, suggesting LMs develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.conclusion: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across modalities, indicating that LMs may internally develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.key_findings:
Brain regions with higher semantic consistency (responding similarly to concepts across text and image paradigms) are better predicted by LM representations.
This correlation holds even in brain regions with weak language selectivity.
Representational similarity between LMs and semantically consistent brain regions is significant and increases for vision-language models when using both text and image stimuli.
Both language-only and vision-language models show alignment with semantically consistent brain regions.
papers.limitation:
The picture paradigm correlation is lower and skewed by visual cortex areas that encode images but not necessarily concepts.
